title: A Super-Secret Spy Tool Is About to Expire—What Happens Now?
summary: Imagine if the government had a special tool to listen to bad guys' phone calls and read their emails from far away. That tool exists, and it's called Section 702. But here's the twist: it's about to expire! Section 702 lets U.S. spy agencies collect electronic messages from people outside America—like suspected terrorists or hackers. Every year, a secret court approves it. But Congress couldn't agree on new rules before the deadline on Friday. So, will the spying stop? Not exactly. The law says companies like phone and internet providers must keep handing over information until the current court order runs out. That could be months. But some lawmakers worry that companies might challenge the law in court, causing a pause. Experts say that's unlikely, and if it happens, a court could fix it in 30 days. One former NSA lawyer said it's not a disaster, but it's still irresponsible to take any risk when Congress could have just extended it. The bigger fight is about privacy. When the U.S. collects messages from foreigners, it sometimes catches Americans' texts and emails too. Some lawmakers want a warrant before the FBI can look at that info. That debate got messy when President Trump picked a controversial new intelligence boss, and Democrats said they wouldn't renew the law while he's in charge. So for now, the spy tool stays on—but with a lot of drama behind the scenes.
why_it_matters: Just like you have a right to keep your diary private, this story shows how countries balance safety and the right to privacy, which affects everyone in the digital world.

background_read: Section 702 is part of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA), created after the terrorist attacks of 9/11 to help catch threats from overseas.
The National Security Agency (NSA), one of America's top spy agencies, uses Section 702 to collect emails and phone data from foreigners abroad.
Every year, a special secret court called the FISA Court checks whether the program is following the rules, but it rarely stops it.
Article_Structure: WHO: U.S. spy agencies, Congress, President Trump, Democrats, the FBI, and a former NSA lawyer.
WHAT: Section 702, a law allowing spying on foreigners' electronic messages, is about to expire, but companies must keep providing data until the court order ends.
WHERE: In the United States, affecting how spy agencies work.
WHY: To catch terrorists and hackers overseas, but there is debate over privacy because it can also collect Americans' private chats without a warrant.

perspectives.description: Security experts argue that Section 702 is vital to detect terrorist plots and keep the country safe.
Privacy advocates worry that innocent Americans' information could be swept up without a judge's approval, which is unfair.
Lawmakers are stuck between keeping the tool active and adding stronger privacy protections, leading to a messy debate.
